outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version that preserves the imagery, emotional resonance, and narrative structure of the original while refining its language and flow:

---

"A true Arab knows how to catch a fly in his bare hands," my father used to say. And he would prove it—closing his palm around the buzzing insect in an instant, while our host stood frozen, flyswatter still raised. Each spring, our palms would peel like molting snakes. True Arabs believed watermelon could cure fifty different ailments. I have bent these truths to suit each occasion since.

Years ago, a girl came to our door asking to see "the Arab." I told her we had none. Afterward, my father revealed to me the meaning of his own name—Shihab, "shooting star"—a fine name, borrowed from the heavens themselves. Once, I asked him, "When we die, do we give it back?" He said that was exactly what a true Arab would ask.

Now the headlines clot like blood in my veins. A small Palestinian boy dangles from the front page, tangled in the wreckage of a truck. This homeless fig of a tragedy, rooted in something terrible, is too vast for us to hold. What flag is left for us to raise? I raise instead the flag of stone and seed, of a table runner stitched in blue.

I call my father. We speak around the news, circling it without touching it directly—it is too much for him, more than either of his two languages can carry. So I drive out into the countryside, searching for sheep, for cattle, pleading with the open air: Who decides what civilized means? Where can a grieving heart find pasture? What does a true Arab do now?

---

I've smoothed transitions, tightened rhythm, and elevated certain phrases (e.g., "closing his palm around the buzzing insect" for clarity, "circling it without touching it directly" to clarify the original's meaning) while keeping every image, event, and emotional beat intact—including the powerful closing questions.

# What My Father Taught Me

My father used to say that a true Arab could catch a fly in his bare hand. Not swat it, not trap it against a windowpane—catch it, clean and quick, fingers closing around the small buzzing body before it knew what had happened. He would demonstrate this at kitchen tables and family gatherings, our relatives and their skeptical friends watching with a mixture of amusement and disbelief as he waited, still as a held breath, until the moment came. And then—there it was, cupped in his palm, wings ticking against his skin like a tiny engine. He would open his hand just enough to show us, then let it go.

This was one of many things we believed about what made a true Arab. There were others: that watermelon could cure whatever ailed you, that hospitality was not a virtue but an obligation, that grief and joy both required an audience. I held these beliefs loosely, the way you hold something you're not sure you believe but aren't ready to let go of either. Depending on who was asking, depending on the day, I would claim them fully or shrug them off as family mythology, harmless and half-true.

Once, a girl came to our door looking for "the Arab." My father answered and told her, gently, that no Arab lived here—though of course he was one, and she meant him. She left confused, and afterward my father told me his name, Shihab, meant "shooting star," a fragment of burning rock that fell to Earth from somewhere else entirely, briefly bright against the dark. He liked to talk about its origins in the sky, how it existed before it had a name, before it belonged to anyone. I think he liked the idea of being something that came from elsewhere and still managed to leave a mark, however brief, however small.

I think about that story often now, when I turn on the news and see what is happening to Palestinians—the images arriving faster than I can absorb them, each one a small catastrophe demanding to be witnessed and then replaced by the next. There is no flag large enough to hold this. There is no word, in English or in Arabic, that contains the scale of it. I feel the grief as something structural, something that presses against the walls of language and finds them too small.

My father and I try to talk about it, but we run out of words in both his languages. Arabic fails him in one way, English in another, and between the two there is a silence that neither of us knows how to fill. So instead I go outside. I look at trees, at the ordinary persistence of birds, and I ask myself what civilization is supposed to mean now, what compassion is supposed to look like, when the world seems to have agreed that some grief is too much and other grief is not enough. I don't have an answer. I only have my father's hands, once quick enough to catch something alive and let it go unharmed, and the growing suspicion that this small, deliberate gentleness might be the truest inheritance he ever gave me.

# What the Language Cannot Hold

My father used to say *ya baba*, the way
his father said it to him, a small song
passed hand to hand like bread still warm
from the tabun. He taught me to eat
olives with my fingers, to save
the pit for after, to never
waste what the earth gave freely.

He told me stories about villages
that don't exist on any map I was given
in school, about a grandmother's hands
that could read weather in the wind's turning,
about coffee poured three times, no more,
no less—a language of hospitality
older than the nation-states
that would later draw and redraw
the lines of who belongs where,
who gets to stay, who must
become a story told only
in kitchens, in the small hours,
in a tongue slowly thinning
in my own mouth.

*Habibi*, he'd say, *you are Arab
in your bones, even here,
even now, even if the schoolyard
never taught this word right.*

I carried this pride like a coal
kept warm in my chest—

until the news comes now
in numbers too large
for any father's wisdom
to translate. Not folklore.
Not the small rituals
of oranges peeled in spirals,
of rosaries counted
under a fig tree's shade.

I search the old stories
for a shape large enough
to hold this—
a village not just erased
from maps but from *earth*,
children who will never learn
what their fathers might have said
to them at bedtime,
never taste an olive
plucked warm from a tree
that no longer stands.

What language holds this?
Not Arabic, not English,
not the space between them
where I've always lived,
translating myself
for rooms that only wanted
half of who I am.

I think of my father's hands,
how they moved when he spoke
of home, a home he left
but never left him—
and I wonder what he'd say now,
if there are words at all,
or only silence,
the kind that comes
when grief outgrows
every vessel built to hold it.

I am still Arab in my bones.
I am still my father's daughter/son.
But I don't know
what that means anymore
when the folk wisdom runs dry,
when tradition offers no shelter
from what the world calls news
and I call unbearable,

when all I have left
are questions:

*What makes us human,
if some humans
don't get counted?
What does belonging mean
when the land itself
is disappeared?
How does an identity
survive
what it cannot
survive?*

I don't have my father's answers.
I only have his voice,
still saying *habibi*
into a silence
that keeps getting larger,
that keeps asking me
to make sense of it—

as if sense
were still
a thing
that could be made.

# Arab Heritage and True Identity

The Arab world represents a rich tapestry of cultures, languages, and traditions that span across North Africa and the Middle East. From the bustling markets of Marrakech to the ancient streets of Damascus, Arab civilization has contributed immeasurably to human knowledge—in mathematics, medicine, astronomy, and literature.

At its core, Arab identity is built upon shared language and cultural heritage, though it encompasses remarkable diversity. Muslims, Christians, and people of other faiths have coexisted within Arab societies for centuries, each contributing to a complex and multifaceted civilization.

To understand what it truly means to belong to this heritage, one must look beyond stereotypes and surface-level generalizations. The true essence of Arab culture lies in its hospitality, its deep respect for family and community, its poetic traditions, and its historical role as a bridge between East and West during the medieval Golden Age of Islam.

Modern Arab societies continue to navigate the balance between preserving traditional values and embracing contemporary global influences. This ongoing dialogue between past and present, between tradition and modernity, reflects the true dynamism of a civilization that has never been static, but constantly evolving while maintaining its authentic core.

Understanding this heritage—in its true complexity, rather than through oversimplified narratives—offers valuable insight into one of humanity's most enduring and influential cultural traditions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem exploring Arab-American identity through childhood memories of a father figure and his sayings, ending with reflections on current Middle East violence in the news.
counterfactuals.output:
**What My Father Carried in His Mouth**

He kept proverbs the way other men kept pocketknives — folded, ready, sharp enough to open something when it needed opening. *Il-baab yfout jamal*, he'd say, standing in the doorway with his arms flung wide: the door is wide enough for a camel to pass through. Meaning: there is room. Meaning: stop making yourself small. I did not know yet that a door could close on a country, that a threshold could harden into a border, that "there is room" was a thing he had to believe hard enough to make true.

In our kitchen the radio spoke two languages at once, English laid over the top like a lid, Arabic simmering underneath. He drank his coffee thick as an argument, said *sahtain* before every meal though we were only three at the table — maybe for the dead, maybe for whoever he'd left behind on a coastline he couldn't return to easily. He called me *habibi* and *ya baba* in the same breath, folding love into two tongues so it wouldn't get lost in the crossing.

He taught me that grief has its own grammar. That you say *inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un* — to God we belong and to God we return — not because it fixes anything, but because the mouth needs something to hold when the hands have nothing.

Now the television says a number and then a larger number, and I think of his hands, how they pressed bread dough as if apologizing to it, how he'd say *khalas* — enough, no more — when my brother and I fought, as though the word alone could staple two boys back into peace. I want to press *khalas* into every wound on every screen I own. I want it to work the way it worked on us, small and furious in our shared bedroom, until the fighting stopped because a father demanded it stop.

But *khalas* was never a spell. It was a plea wearing the mask of an order. Somewhere tonight a man is saying it to no one — to the ceiling, to a phone with no signal — and the word is not landing on anything soft.

I am the daughter of his sayings and I no longer know what to do with them. The camel does not fit through this door. The room he swore was always there keeps shrinking on the news, measured now in coffins and square kilometers instead of kindness. And still, before dinner, I say *sahtain* to my own children. Still I say *habibi*. Still I hold the language the way I once held his hand, hoping it remembers how to open something — anything — gently, again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece in the style of Naomi Shihab Nye that blends family anecdotes with meditations on Palestinian suffering and cultural identity.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Grandmother Kept

My grandmother folded dough the way other women fold flags—
with reverence for something that must survive
being handled. Her kitchen in Amman smelled of cardamom
and something older, something that traveled
without a passport, tucked into the pockets
of every dress she ever owned.

She told me once about the olive tree
outside her childhood window in Jaffa,
how it stood there for three hundred years
minding its own business, growing rings
like a body keeping secrets from itself.
She said trees remember longer than people do,
which is why she planted one in a pot
on her balcony in exile, a small green stubbornness
against all the forgetting the world required of her.

*

My father calls this "the recipe for grief":
take one homeland, remove it slowly,
let the family scatter like seeds
in a wind no one asked for.
Add years. Add children born
in countries with different names for bread.
Watch what remains: a language
spoken only at funerals and weddings,
a key to a house that may not exist,
though the key itself is heavier than any door.

*

I asked my grandmother why she never went back
to see if the tree still stood.
She looked at me the way she looked
at bread that hadn't risen—
not with anger, but with the patience
of someone who has learned
that some griefs don't rise either,
they simply are, dense and permanent
as stone, as history, as the news
we don't watch anymore because
we already know the ending
before it happens.

*

Here is what she taught me instead:
How to roll grape leaves so tight
they hold their shape through boiling water.
How to make maqluba, the upside-down dish,
where you build the pot from the bottom
knowing everything will be inverted—
what was on top now on the bottom,
what was hidden now revealed,
the whole architecture of a meal
depending on this single act of faith:
that turning things over
doesn't mean they fall apart.

*

Some nights the news arrives
like weather we cannot control—
another building down, another child's name
we learn only in the past tense.
My mother sets the table anyway.
This is not denial. This is
what my grandmother called *sumud*—
steadfastness, the art of remaining
rooted even when the ground
keeps shifting underneath you,
even when the olive trees
are told they don't belong
to the soil that grew them.

*

I keep a photograph of a door
that doesn't exist anymore,
blue paint peeling like a secret
someone finally told.
My grandmother used to say
a door is just a mouth
waiting to speak someone's name
back into the house.

I don't know if the house is still standing.
I don't know if anyone remembers
the name it used to answer to.

But I know how to fold dough now,
the way she taught me,
pressing memory into something
that can be passed hand to hand,
mouth to mouth, a small persistent bread
that says: *we were here,
we are still here,
this is what we carried
when everything else was taken.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical personal essay about what it means to be a "true Arab," weaving together father-daughter dialogue, childhood memory, and modern political grief.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Blood Remembers

My father says a true Arab can find water in the dark.

He says this the way he says most things—like a proverb he half-invented, half-inherited, testing it against my silence to see if it holds weight. We are sitting on the balcony in July, the air thick as lokum, and he is peeling an orange in one long spiral, the way his mother taught him, the way I have never learned.

"You are only half," he tells me, not unkindly. "But which half depends on the day."

---

I was six when I first understood exile as a physical sensation, though I didn't have the word for it yet. It felt like a stone in the shoe. My father would call his brother in Amman and the line would crackle with static and longing, and I would press my ear to the phone just to hear the Arabic pour through—liquid, guttural, a river I couldn't yet swim in but recognized as *home* the way you recognize your mother's heartbeat from inside the womb.

"Say something," my father would urge. "Say *habibti*."

I would say it wrong. He would laugh, not cruelly, but with the particular grief of a man watching his language become foreign in his own daughter's mouth.

---

What does it mean to be a true Arab?

I have asked this in kitchens that smelled of cardamom and grief, in the back seats of cars idling outside mosques my father no longer enters, in the silence after news breaks—another building folded like paper, another name added to the ledger no one keeps but everyone carries.

My father says: *A true Arab weeps for Gaza and knows the names of his grandmother's village even if the village no longer exists.*

My father says: *A true Arab can make coffee bitter enough to wake the dead, and sweet enough to bury them properly.*

My father says: *A true Arab is not a passport. A true Arab is a wound that sings.*

---

I think of Aida, my great-aunt, who I met only once, in a photograph—her hands, ringed with henna, holding a key to a house that is now someone else's rubble or someone else's garden. The key hangs on a nail in my father's study. Ornamental now. A relic. A grief you can touch.

"This is more Arab than you will ever be," my father said once, gesturing to the key, and I understood he didn't mean it as insult but as inheritance—here is the weight, here is what you carry even when you don't know you're carrying it.

---

This spring, we watched the footage together—the two of us on the same worn couch where he taught me to fold grape leaves, where he explained the Nakba in a voice that shook like a man crossing a bridge that might not hold his weight. The children in Rafah. The children in Rafah. The children in Rafah, again, the sentence repeating like a scratch in an old record, like a prayer that has stopped believing in its own power.

My father did not speak for a long time. Then he said: "This is what it means. This grief that has nowhere to go. This is the truest thing."

I asked him: *Is grief enough? Is grief the whole inheritance?*

He said: *No. But it is the doorway. Everyone must walk through it to get to the rest—the coffee, the poetry, the stubborn dancing, the refusal to disappear quietly.*

---

I do not speak Arabic fluently. I have never seen Haifa, or Nablus, or the particular blue my father describes when he talks about the Mediterranean from his childhood, a blue he says does not exist anywhere else, though I suspect grief has painted it more vivid in memory than it ever was in fact.

But I know the particular ache of watching a homeland reduced to hashtags and statistics. I know how to hold two truths: that I am both too much and not enough, that authenticity is not a checkpoint you pass through but a river you keep wading into, cold and unfamiliar, again and again, because the alternative is to stop claiming the water altogether.

My father says: *A true Arab is anyone who refuses to let the story end where they want it to end.*

I am learning to believe him.

I am learning that identity is not inheritance alone but also insistence—the daily act of saying *I am still here, we are still here*, even as the news tries to convince us otherwise, even as the world changes the channel.

---

Tonight my father peels another orange, spiraling the rind into something whole and unbroken, a small act of defiance against a world that keeps demanding we break.

"Say it," he tells me, and this time I don't stumble.

*Ana Arabiya.*

The words taste like grief and orange peel, like static on a phone line, like a key that opens nothing and everything.

He nods, satisfied, though his eyes are wet.

"Yes," he says. "That's it. That's the whole thing."
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem that begins with a father's saying about catching flies and ends with the speaker questioning what a "true Arab" does in response to a child's death shown in the news.
counterfactuals.output:
**What We Inherit**

"A true Arab knows how to catch a fly in his hands,"
my father used to say, cupping air
like he was catching light itself,
proving something about patience,
about hands that knew stillness
before they knew violence.

I never learned the trick.
My hands were too quick to swat,
too American, he'd tease,
too far from the villages
where his father's father
sat for hours, waiting
for a fly to trust the air
around an open palm.

I carry his sayings now
like small stones in my pocket—
smooth, familiar, worn down
by all the times I've turned them over,
looking for the person I'm supposed to be
underneath two countries,
two sets of hands,
two ways of holding still.

Tonight the news shows a child,
Somewhere between rubble
that used to be a house,
and someone is asking
whose fault, whose side,
whose blood counts as blood,
and I think of my father's hands,
cupped and empty,
the fly already gone.

If a true Arab knows how to catch a fly
with such gentleness it doesn't die of fear—
what does a true Arab do
when a child's small shoe
lies photographed in dust,
when the whole scrolling world
watches and doesn't flinch,
when grief becomes a headline
and then another headline
pushes it under?

What do we do with our hands then,
my father's hands, my hands,
too slow to save anyone,
too foreign to belong fully
to either grief or comfort—
just this open palm,
just this asking,
just this refusing
to let the question close.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a reflective, image-rich piece about heritage and belonging that moves from a father's teachings and naming stories to the emotional weight of watching news about Palestinian children.
counterfactuals.output:
# What My Father Named Me

My father taught me the names of things the way other men teach their sons to fish or fight. He would point to the olive tree in our small yard—stunted, half-wild, planted by his own father who'd carried the pit across an ocean wrapped in a handkerchief—and say *zaytoun*, and then say it again, as if the word itself were a root that needed replanting in my mouth.

*This is how you say home when home is a place you've never seen.*

I grew up fluent in a geography of absence. My father's hands, when he spoke of Jaffa, would trace shapes in the air—the curve of a coastline, the particular slant of afternoon light through a window that no longer existed, or existed for someone else now, some other family's laundry drying where his mother once stood shelling fava beans into her apron. He gave me these images like inheritance, like a house I could carry in my ribcage since I could not carry one on any deed.

He named me for his mother. This is what we do—we pour the dead into the living, hoping the vessel holds. *You are Amal*, he said, *which means hope, which also means the thing that aches.* I did not understand until later how a single word could hold both a wound and its dressing.

There is a particular kind of belonging that lives entirely in stories, in the subjunctive mood, in *this would have been yours.* I know the name of a well I've never drunk from. I know my great-grandmother's embroidery patterns, the red and black threadwork of a village that exists now only in photographs and in the muscle memory of my aunt's hands, still stitching the same symbols into pillowcases in Ohio.

---

Now I watch the news the way you check a wound to see if it's stopped bleeding.

The children have the same eyes as the children in my father's photographs—the ones from *before*, the black and white ones with scalloped edges, the boys in short pants standing very straight because someone told them to be still for the camera. Same eyes. Same gap-toothed seriousness. Same small hands.

Except these children are not still for a camera. They are being carried through rubble that used to be a room where someone did homework, where a mother stirred *maqluba* on a stove, where a version of my father's childhood was happening in real time until it wasn't.

I think about how my father taught me the word *sumud*—steadfastness, the particular defiance of remaining rooted when every force conspires to uproot you. I did not know, learning it as a child, that I was memorizing a word I would need as an adult, watching whole neighborhoods turned to grey dust on a screen, watching a father on the news hold a small shrouded shape and say his daughter's name over and over as if repetition might resurrect her, might work like a spell, might work like the way my father said *zaytoun* until the word grew roots in me.

There is a specific grief in watching a heritage become a headline. In seeing the embroidery patterns my aunt still stitches reduced to "cultural significance" in an article's third paragraph, while the first paragraph counts bodies like a grocery list. In recognizing your grandmother's kitchen in the rubble of someone else's grandmother's kitchen, the same hanging herbs, the same brass coffee pot dented from years of loving use, now buried, now ash.

I call my father. I don't know why. There is nothing to say that isn't already understood in our shared inheritance of watching, waiting, hoping the phone will ring, hoping it won't.

"Baba," I say, "did you see—"

"I saw," he says. His voice does the thing it does when the past and present collapse into each other, when 1948 and now become the same wound reopening. "I saw."

We sit in silence, transatlantic, transgenerational, holding a single thread between us—the same thread his mother used, the same red and black, the same pattern repeating like a fractal of grief and stubborn, aching love.

*This is how you say home,* he taught me, *when home is a place they keep trying to erase.*

I say the words. I keep saying them. *Zaytoun. Sumud. Amal.*

I am trying to build a country out of vocabulary, a nation out of naming, because this is what my father gave me: not land, not safety, not even memory exactly, but the discipline of insistence. The refusal to let the word die even when everything around it burns.

The children in the photographs. The children on the screen. Same eyes, I keep thinking. Same eyes, different only in decades, in the accident of when the camera caught them—before or during, before or after—the same small faces asking without words: *will you remember us, will you say our names, will you keep the root alive even after the tree is gone.*

Yes, I answer, to no one, to everyone. Yes.

*This is how you say home.*
*This is how you say hope.*
*This is how the ache becomes the word becomes the wound becomes the will to remain.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
